title: Faith rests on the speaker's authority, not on evidence in the things; formal object is divine revelation
source_text: XXVII. Primo enim hactenus in Scholis receptum est fidem, licet non excludat ratiocinationes, potius tamen loquentis authoritate niti. Sed authoritate divina potissimum non nititur fides, si praecipua ratio, cur rebus fidei credimus, sit quaedam, quae ipsis inest, evidentia veritatis, non divina revelatio. Absurda quoque esset fidei definitio, nempe, quod sit assensus quem Deo loquenti praebemus. Tum enim per fidem Deo loquenti non crederemus, nisi materialiter, ut dicitur in Scholis, hoc est, crederemus quidem iis, quae Deus loqueretur, at non, quia Deus illa locutus esset. Sed absurde mentis aliquis habitus ab objecto suo tantum materiali definitur. Si quis enim, verbi causa, Peripateticae doctrinae peritus incidat in aliquem librum Aristotelis, et doctrinam illius exacte considerans, veram esse agnoscat, atque etiam ex acumine styli et differendi modo judicet librum esse Aristotelis, assensus illi doctrinae praebitus nonnisi absurde dici poterit fides Aristoteli dicenti habita. At certe Theologi huc usque communi consensu, non tantum fidem definiunt assensum Deo loquenti exhibitum, et statuunt objectum illius esse Dei verbum, et res a Deo revelatas; sed etiam objecti illius rationem formalem, sub qua fides illud apprehendit, et ob quam illud recipit et agnoscit, docent esse divinam authoritatem et revelationem.
pass_a_gloss: For first, up to now it has been received in the Schools that faith, although it does not exclude reasonings, nevertheless rather rests on the authority of the one speaking. But faith does not rest chiefly on divine authority if the principal reason why we believe the things of faith is a certain evidence of truth which is in them, not divine revelation. The definition of faith would also be absurd, namely that it is the assent which we give to God speaking. For then through faith we would not believe God speaking except materially, as it is said in the Schools, that is, we would indeed believe the things which God would speak, but not because God had spoken them. But absurdly is any habit of the mind defined from its object only as material. For if someone, for example, skilled in Peripatetic doctrine should happen upon some book of Aristotle, and considering its doctrine exactly should recognize it to be true, and should even judge from the sharpness of style and manner of arguing that the book is Aristotle's, the assent given to that doctrine could only absurdly be called faith held toward Aristotle speaking. But certainly the Theologians up to now by common consensus not only define faith as assent exhibited to God speaking, and state that its object is God's Word and things revealed by God; but they also teach that the formal ground of that object, under which faith apprehends it, and on account of which it receives and acknowledges it, is divine authority and revelation.
pass_b_english: First: up to now the Schools have held that faith, though it does not shut out reasoning, rests rather on the authority of the one who speaks. But faith does not rest chiefly on divine authority if the principal reason we believe the things of faith is a certain evidence of truth in the things themselves, not divine revelation. The definition of faith would also become absurd — that it is the assent we give to God speaking. For then through faith we would believe God speaking only materially, as the Schools say: we would believe the things God spoke, but not because God had spoken them. And it is absurd to define any habit of mind from its object only as material.

Suppose someone skilled in Peripatetic doctrine happens on a book of Aristotle, studies its teaching carefully, recognizes it as true, and even judges from the sharpness of style and manner of arguing that the book is Aristotle's. The assent he gives that doctrine could only absurdly be called faith held toward Aristotle speaking. Yet up to now the Theologians by common consensus not only define faith as assent exhibited to God speaking, and take its object to be God's Word and things revealed by God; they also teach that the formal ground of that object — under which faith apprehends it, and on account of which it receives and acknowledges it — is divine authority and revelation.
